notes.text: The filter on orders kept 74.4% of rows. With that many matches an index scan would fetch most pages anyway, so the optimizer would likely keep the sequential scan. No index suggested.

QueryLab joins with hash or nested-loop joins and never uses an index to look up join partners, so an index on the join key would not change this join. (Engines with index nested-loop joins, such as PostgreSQL, can benefit.)

events.note: Events were recorded on the real execution path and are replayed after the query finished.

facts.text: Return c.city, COUNT(*) AS n from orders, joined with customers on o.customer_id = c.id, keeping only rows where o.total > 900, grouped by c.city, sorted by n (descending), returning at most 3 rows.
Table orders (as o) has 10,000 rows in 147 pages; the query reads 2 of its 5 columns (customer_id, total).
Table customers (as c) has 1,000 rows in 15 pages; the query reads 2 of its 5 columns (id, city).
The sequential scan of orders read 147 pages (0 not in the buffer pool) and examined 10,000 rows; the filter o.total > 900 kept 7,440 (74.4%) and discarded 2,560.
The sequential scan of customers read 15 pages (15 not in the buffer pool) and examined 1,000 rows.

Sequential scan of orders: no index matches the query's predicates. Considered: Index Scan using idx_orders_customer_id — not applicable: no equality or range predicate on its leading column 'customer_id'.
Sequential scan of customers: the table has no indexes.
Hash Join (build on c) has the lowest estimated cost (168.6).
Physical operators, in the order they produce rows: Seq Scan (o) → Seq Scan (c) → Hash Join → Hash Aggregate → Project → Sort → Limit.
Rows produced by each operator: Seq Scan (o): 7,440 → Seq Scan (c): 1,000 → Hash Join: 7,440 → Hash Aggregate: 16 → Project: 16 → Sort: 3 → Limit: 3. The query returned 3 rows.
Most measured time was spent in Seq Scan (o): 3.811 ms of 7.609 ms of operator time (50.1%). It read 147 pages.

Engine execution took 7.717 ms (excluding parsing, planning, JSON encoding and network). Per-operator timers were read 31,876 times at ~22 ns each, so roughly 0.701 ms of the measured time is instrumentation overhead.

guidance: Indexes help most when a filter keeps a small fraction of a large table. When most rows match, a sequential scan is usually cheaper because it reads each page once, in order.
Sort must consume its entire input before returning the first row. Here LIMIT sits above Sort, so it reduces the rows returned but not the rows sorted.
explanation.summary: Returned 3 rows in 7.717 ms after examining 11,000 stored rows across 162 page accesses.
